title: One task, different choices: comparing three providers

opening.headline: When ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini all have similar features, let's look at what to compare them based on, not just their names.
body: Requests to find multiple materials and organize them with evidence can be made through any service. All three services guide you through functions such as search, in-depth research, and connecting to external apps, but because they have different names and screens, it is difficult to see at a glance what is the same and what is different.

In this lesson, you will learn how to map features by role instead of feature name. It puts the three services side by side with five roles: conversation, search, research, project, and connection, and at the end, we see an explanation of how the three services implement the same task of organizing weekly reports.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Conversation, search, research, project, and connection functions can be supported by the three companies.
Can judge the basis of selection criteria such as work, environment, and authority

screens.title: Three companies, similar features, different names
screens.lead: Assuming the same request is made to all three services, read the scene below and think about what makes it difficult to compare.

visual.alt: A scene where three columns of ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini are placed side by side under the same request sentence, and different function names are written in each column.

paragraphs: Let’s think about a common request at work. This is a request to find various materials and organize them with evidence. ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini all provide features that help with this.

The problem is the name. One service calls it deep research, another service calls it research, and yet another service calls it Deep Research. Some features are search-focused, while others are geared toward creating reports across multiple sources. Just by looking at the names, it's hard to know which one fits this need.
There is only one question in this class. What should we compare, not the function name? The answer lies in roles, not names.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Are choosing a service with many features the same thing as choosing a service that suits my job? You will be able to answer this question at the end of the lesson.

screens.outro: First, let's recall our experience comparing services so far.

screens.title: Recall the standards by which services were compared
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: If you were to compare two services that you have used so far, what criteria did you use to compare them?
items.answer: It's easy for obvious criteria to come to mind first, such as speed, price, attribution, and file handling. All of these standards are meaningful, but the names and scope of the functions for each service are different, so comparisons may be inconsistent. In this class, we organize this into the framework of work, environment, and authority.

items.prompt: Did you think that functions with the same name would do the same thing?
items.answer: Even if the name is the same, the scope of the source and the form of the result may be different. Conversely, there are functions that perform the same role even if their names are different. So it's safer to compare by what you enter and what you receive rather than by name.

The convenient service varies depending on the work environment in which emails and documents are sent. Services that can connect to the environment where the data resides often make the same task much easier.

screens.outro: To organize the criteria we came up with, let's start by looking at a table that shows the features side by side by role.

screens.title: Feature Correspondence Table: Side by Side by Role
screens.lead: Each row in the table is a role, and each column is a function that plays that role for each service. Read the rows horizontally and notice that although the names are different, the roles are the same.

screens.outro: If we correspond to roles, let's point out what actually changes within the same role.

screens.title: Even similar functions are different
screens.lead: Select an underlined passage in the description below to see an explanation of the point of comparison. Please pay attention to the scope of the source and the type of result.

data.text: Claude directs web search to the appropriate feature in Fact-checking answers with just one or two tool calls. Extended thinking is suitable for Issues to consider in depth without up-to-date web information. Research matches well with the broad investigation in Create a report by combining multiple sources with five or more tool calls. Gemini's Deep Research defaults to Google Search as a source and uses You can add Gmail, Drive, or uploaded files as sources.. ChatGPT's deep research also reads multiple online sources and synthesizes them into Structured results with citations.

marks.span: Fact-checking answers with just one or two tool calls
marks.note: This is the scope of search for light questions. This includes questions like weather or the latest news, and is not a feature that expects report-level synthesis.

marks.span: Issues to consider in depth without up-to-date web information
marks.note: Extended thinking is not intended to be a web search, but rather a feature that allows you to make deeper inferences. Although it has a similar name to Search, its role is different.

marks.span: Create a report by combining multiple sources with five or more tool calls
marks.note: The characteristics of research are the number of sources and the form of the results. It takes a long time, but the biggest difference from a search is that you receive a report with citations.

marks.span: You can add Gmail, Drive, or uploaded files as sources.
marks.note: Gemini allows you to change the source range directly. You can even turn off Google Search and only use selected sources, allowing you to tailor your research to focus on internal sources.

This is the type of output that the research functions of the three services commonly target. Even if the names are different, it becomes easier to respond if you compare the results as reports with citations.

screens.outro: Let's move on to examples, remembering that the difference is not in the name but in the scope of the source, the result, and the environment in which it is written.

screens.title: Commentary: Implementing weekly reporting as a 3rd party function
screens.lead: The instructor explains step by step the process of implementing the same task in three services. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: organize your demands
steps.body: You need to compile scattered notes and meeting materials and create a weekly report. Before choosing a service name, consider what role this request covers.

steps.title: Break it down into roles
steps.body: Weekly reporting is divided into four roles: Gathering data is a connection, updating information is searching, drafting is a conversation, and repeating the same format every week is a project. By dividing it this way, it becomes clear which functions will be used for each service.

steps.title: In Claude, the format is maintained as projects.
steps.body: Claude's projects is a workspace with its own chat history and knowledge base. If you write down the format and tone of your report in the guidelines and upload past materials, you can receive drafts in the same format every week. If you need more external evidence, choose web search or research according to the situation.

steps.title: Gemini uses linked data as a source.
steps.body: If you connect the Workspace app to Gemini, you can use Gmail and Drive as sources. If you want to organize only internal data, turn off Google Search and use only selected sources. If you need external evidence, reinforce it with Deep Research.

steps.title: ChatGPT combines connection apps and search.
steps.body: In ChatGPT, data from external apps is loaded using a connection app, and parts that require up-to-date information are supplemented with Search. Use deep research when you need structured results that synthesize multiple sources.

steps.title: Check the selection criteria
steps.body: All three services can get the job done, so your final choice will come down to criteria rather than number of features. What is the work content, what work environment is the data in, and what permissions are allowed. If the data is already in the Google environment and connection is allowed, Gemini is close, and if the format needs to be maintained for a long time, Claude with projects is close. The key to this judgment is not whether there is one correct answer, but whether the standard can be explained in words.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed that the same task is implemented with different functions for each service, we will summarize the criteria for judgment.

screens.title: Compare roles and choose based on criteria
screens.lead: I will organize what I have seen so far into one judgment framework. Read it while thinking about the tasks you repeat.

paragraphs: Compare services by role, not feature name. Divided into five roles: conversation, search, research, project, and connection, the functions of the three services meet on one table.

During the selection stage, we check three criteria. What results is required by the work content, what environment is the data in, and is permission to read or write the data permitted? If you use in-depth research for a task that only requires light fact-checking, you will waste time, and if you use a simple search for a task that requires synthesizing multiple sources, you will lack evidence.

Please also remember that even with similar functions, the source scope and output form are different. The correspondence table serves as a guide when changing services. However, since the table is only a starting point, the most accurate comparison is to make the same request to both services and directly compare the form and source indication of the results.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: The service with the most features isn't always the best. A service that matches the environment where my work and data are located and the permissions granted is a more appropriate choice. Check yourself to see if you can give these three reasons for your choice.

glossary.def: This is a table where functions with different names are arranged side by side based on their roles.
This is an in-depth research function that reads and synthesizes multiple sources and organizes them into a report. Each service has a different name.
Claude's features tie your materials, instructions, and chat history into one workspace.
The criteria for selecting a service are the job description, the environment used, and the permissions granted.

misconceptions.myth: If the function name is the same, it works the same way.
misconceptions.fact: The scope of origin, results, and usage environment may vary from service to service. Compare input and output rather than name.

misconceptions.myth: The service with the most features is always best.
misconceptions.fact: A service tailored to the environment where the work and data are located is more appropriate. Having a lot of features you won't use is not an advantage.

misconceptions.myth: Search and research are the same function.
misconceptions.fact: Search is a light fact-check that requires one or two tool calls, while research is research that involves going back and forth between multiple sources to create a comprehensive report.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Compare by role (Conversation, Search, Research, Project, Connect) rather than feature name.
Selection criteria are the content of the work, the environment in which the material is located, and the permissions granted.
Similar functions have different sources and output types.
The correspondence table serves as a guide when changing services.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What functions of the three services correspond to the needs of my repetitive work?

checks.q: What type of function best fits the need to read widely from multiple sources and report with citations?
options: Ability to synthesize multiple sources, such as research (deep research, etc.)
Ability to check facts with one or two tool calls, like a search
Ability to think deeply without the latest web information, such as extended thinking
A workspace where materials and instructions are grouped together like a project.
checks.explain: The role of the research function is to conduct extensive research across multiple sources and produce results.

wrong.1: Search is good for light fact-checking and not enough for report-level synthesis.
wrong.2: Extended thinking is different from source synthesis because it involves examining in depth without web information.
wrong.3: A project is a space to store data and is not a function of conducting research itself.

checks.intro: Check out the feature comparison you just saw for yourself. Results are not recorded, and commentary appears immediately after you select an option.

checks.q: Match the roles of weekly reporting tasks with the appropriate functions.
right: Maintain format with guidelines and past data for projects
Find the latest information with the search function
Load data from external apps using the connection function
Refine your draft by asking questions using the conversation function
checks.explain: When tasks are divided into roles, connection, search, conversation, and project correspond to each other. The comparison is by role rather than function name.
